entities.name: Jami Mosque of Pontianak
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Jami Mosque of Pontianak (Indonesian: Masjid Jami' Sultan Syarif Abdurrahman) in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, Indonesia — built in 1771 as the city mosque of the newly founded Sultanate of Pontianak — is one of the oldest extant mosques in Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo) and a monument to the founding of Pontianak by Arab-Malay Sultan Syarif Abdurrahman al-Qadri in 1771, making it among the earliest documented Islamic institutional foundations in Borneo's interior regions.

Pontianak's founding is historically distinctive: the city sits on the equator (making it one of the few cities in the world directly on the equatorial line) and was founded at the confluence of the Kapuas and Landak rivers specifically as a new sultanate capital by Syarif Abdurrahman, who was of Arab (Hadhrami) descent — reflecting the pattern of Arab and Hadhrami merchants and clerics who established Islamic sultanates across maritime Southeast Asia from the 15th-18th centuries. This Arab-Malay expansion of Islam across maritime Southeast Asia was one of the most successful religious expansions in world history.

The Jami Mosque's traditional Malay Islamic architecture — featuring a multi-tiered wooden roof rather than a dome (the characteristic pre-colonial Southeast Asian mosque style before Middle Eastern influences modernized mosque design) — represents the distinctive regional Islamic architectural tradition of maritime Southeast Asia. The mosque has been renovated multiple times but retains its traditional character and continues to serve as Pontianak's central congregational mosque.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Jami Mosque of Pontianak — built in 1771 as a monument to the Arab-Malay Islamic expansion that founded Pontianak as a sultanate capital, one of Borneo's oldest surviving mosques — is historically significant as evidence of the remarkable Islamic expansion across maritime Southeast Asia.
